title: Burst Quota Sculpting & Key Mapping Demo - Veridian Analytics
summary: Introductory demo focused on org vs project key strategies, burst quota sculpting, and mapping keys to SLO tiers. transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-03
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Lena (Redwood), Marco (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood), Rajesh, Emily, Noah, Sofia (Veridian)

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Lena, AE on the Redwood inference team, with Marco our SE and Priya on the solutions side. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Rajesh: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to dig in. We've been evaluating a couple of patterns for tenant throttling and want to see how Redwood handles bursty data enrichment pipelines.
[00:18] Marco: Great, quick agenda. We'll walk through keying patterns (org vs project), quota shaping primitives — think leaky bucket, fairburst — show Console configs, then Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization, and end with pilot options.
[00:30] Emily: Quick note, from SRE perspective our big ask is predictable p95 latency under 100ms for small prompts and reasonable cost. We also need SSO + KMS integration details.
[00:45] Marco: Noted. We'll surface routing and fallback behavior for hosted and Dedicated.

--- Demo section ---
[02:10] Marco: So first slide, org keys give you broad quotas at account level, project keys let you split and isolate workloads. Some customers use org keys for billing and project keys for per-team throttles.
[02:35] Rajesh: Can you do hybrid? Like org-level baseline and project burst allowances?
[02:40] Marco: Yeah that's the typical pattern — baseline org quota plus project-specific concurrency slices. We call it "baseline + sculpt" in internal docs. If you look here in Console — (screen noise) — you can create quota lanes and assign priority.
[03:08] Lena: I'll drop the Console link in the chat after, but the important bit is the enforcement engine supports both token and concurrency quotas, and you can map keys to routing policies.
[03:25] Noah: Do you support sticky routing so a token hits the same back-end when caching is in play?
[03:32] Marco: Yes, sticky routing by org/project key and by model variant. That helps prefix/K-V cache hits — sometimes we see transcriber mislabels it K-V cash — but it's KV cache basically.

[05:00] Marco: Now burst behavior. We use a leaky-bucket style with per-key leaky windows and a global guardrail. So you can allow short high-TPS bursts but then taper to baseline. We also have a fairshare allocator when multiple projects share org capacity.
[05:26] Emily: If one project goes nutty during a flash sale how does it impact others? Can we set per-project backpressure?
[05:32] Marco: Yep, you can set per-project hard concurrency caps and soft burst allowances. If soft bursts exceed, we push 429s or queue depending on route policy, and you can configure automatic fallback to a cheaper quantized model.
[06:00] Rajesh: Automatic fallback sounds good. Is fallback cross-region? We have a data residency constraint for EU traffic.
[06:10] Marco: Fallback respects region pinning; if the model variant isn't available in the region we fall back within the same region or to your Dedicated pool if provisioned. For strict residency you should use Redwood Private or Dedicated with region pinned capacity.

[08:00] Priya: I'll show the Console flow. Here you create an org quota — set monthly token cap, burst window (seconds), and per-project slice. You can also set preemptive throttles by API key label.
[08:24] Sofia: Can the per-project slice be dynamic? Our teams spin up ephemeral projects during experiments.
[08:30] Priya: Yes, you can use tagging + automated policies via the API. Tag a project with "exp:trial" and have a policy granting a temporary burst for X hours.

[10:15] Marco: On the routing side, priority lanes let you move production traffic over guaranteed capacity while letting experimental traffic live on shared hosted lanes. This is how customers get predictable p95.
[10:45] Emily: Are there SLA differences between hosted and Dedicated?
[10:48] Lena: Hosted has best-effort latency targets published; Dedicated has SLA-backed throughput and latency tiers. We can map a Dedicated pool to a project key for guaranteed lanes.

[12:20] Rajesh: Security — we need KMS integration and audit logs, plus SSO (SAML). Any caveats?
[12:30] Marco: Redwood Private and Dedicated both support customer-managed KMS via our KMS connectors (HSM/KMS). Audit logs are available at token-level in Console. SSO via SAML/SCIM for user provisioning. We are SOC 2 Type II — or as some transcribers write, sock two — and can provide the report under NDA.
[13:05] Noah: For KMS, where are keys stored? We prefer keys not leaving our cloud tenant.
[13:12] Marco: With Private/Dedicated you bring your KMS and keys stay in your account. For hosted we integrate via AWS KMS with customer CMKs — the key usage is proxied and logs are kept. We'll put the exact flow in the security packet.

[15:00] Marco: Demoing a quick rule: create project key "payments-processor", set concurrency cap 50, burst allowance 500 tokens per 10s, and route to dedicated-model-1 for production lane. If payments-processor exceeds, route to fallback quantized-3 (cheapest) or enqueue with 10s TTL.
[15:40] Sofia: For billing, does org-level billing capture per-project usage?
[15:45] Lena: Yes, billing granularly attributes tokens to projects and you can export CSVs.

[18:00] Marco: Now about Optimize — the service can recommend quantization levels and batching parameters based on your request shape. For example, Optimize suggested 4-bit quant for one customer whose payloads were small and trimmed cost by 33% without materially impacting quality.
[18:30] Rajesh: Can Optimize run as part of CI? We want to run perf regressions automatically.
[18:36] Marco: Absolutely. Optimize can run periodic evals against a prompt set and alert on quality regressions tied to rollout changes. It's integrated with our rollouts so you can abort a canary if evals drop.

[21:00] Emily: Let's talk pilot specifics. We need a short benchmark with sustained QPS and a spike test. What metrics will Redwood capture?
[21:10] Marco: We'll capture token throughput, p50/p95/p99 latencies, cost per 1k tokens, cache hit ratios, and queueing stats. We'll ship a perf spreadsheet.
[21:28] Rajesh: Can we run it against both hosted and Dedicated to compare?
[21:32] Marco: Yes we'll provision a small Dedicated with pinned region and run identical traffic. We'll also show the fallback scenario where Dedicated is saturated and hosted fallback takes over.

[24:00] Lena: Quick Q&A — Rajesh asked earlier about rate limiting algorithms. We use leaky bucket for steady-state and token-bucket-like accounting for bursts; fairshare for org-level distribution.
[24:22] Noah: Any hard limits on number of project keys? We manage thousands of ephemeral projects.
[24:30] Priya: Scales to tens of thousands of keys; the Console and API support programmatic creation. We do recommend lifecycle cleanup policies.

[27:00] Emily: On error modes: what do users see? 429, 503? Is there a retry guidance?
[27:08] Marco: Mostly 429 for quota, 503 for capacity issues. We provide Retry-After headers and guidance: exponential backoff with jitter, and prefer client-side queueing for predictable UX.

[30:00] Sofia: One more on data residency — we have logs that must not leave EU. How airtight is that?
[30:10] Marco: For strict regulations, Dedicated in-region or Private on-prem ensures logs and data stay within region. Hosted can be configured to store logs in regional buckets but requires review. We'll add details in the security doc.

[33:00] Rajesh: Cost question: how do bursts affect billing? If a project bursts but then refunds tokens via caching, do we bill raw tokens?
[33:10] Marco: Billing is on consumed tokens; KV cache hits reduce token usage. For repeated identical requests, cache reduces billable tokens. We can also apply credits for pilot anomalies if needed — that's part of the commercial conversation.

[36:00] Marco: Now a quick walkthrough of an API flow: you mint project keys under an org, attach tags, hit /v1/generate with header X-Redwood-Key and Redwood routes according to policy. The SDKs support key rotation and automatic retries.
[36:25] Emily: Is key rotation seamless? Will in-flight requests fail?
[36:30] Marco: We support a staged rotation: create new key, update routes, then revoke old. In-flight requests will continue to complete because tokens are valid for N seconds. We'll include rotation best practices.

[39:00] Priya: A couple of realistic gotchas — ephemeral projects can create a lot of keys which complicates RBAC. We recommend a key naming and tag policy and automated cleanup. Also watch KV cache warm-up after a roll.

[41:20] Lena: Ok let's recap. Redwood will: 1) send SOW + pricing, 2) Marco will share perf harness + spreadsheet, 3) Veridian to provide compliance checklist and whitelist IPs. Pilot kickoff planned for week of 3/15.

[41:45] Rajesh: Sounds good. One minute from security: Noah will review the KMS flow and flag anything blocking.
[42:00] Noah: I'll aim to send the checklist by next week.

[44:00] Lena: Anything else?
[44:05] Sofia: No, thanks — appreciate the depth. The console looked straightforward.
[44:12] Priya: We'll follow up with a shared Drive link to the benchmark harness (we'll paste link in chat).

[45:00] Lena: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with next steps and set the pilot calendar.
[45:05] Rajesh: Thanks folks.

End of transcript.
